rationale: Colours 1–4 emit four diagonal rays in their own colours. In demonstration 1, the 8 at row 6 column 2 becomes 3; overlapping rays produce 6, including row 1 column 3.
Demonstration 1 extends 3 and 4 rightward and downward, with 6 at their intersection. Demonstration 3 preserves the 4 beneath the 2 and continues both downward rays to create 6 below it.
Sources emit upward and rightward rays in their own colours. Demonstration 3 overwrites the 8 beside the 1 with 1 and marks intersections with the upward 3 rays as 2.
Demonstration 1 fills the shared column of 2 and 1 with 6 while preserving both sources; the separate 2 fills its column with 2. All 8 cells remain unchanged.
Demonstration 2 has upward and rightward 4 rays intersecting at row 2 column 7 to make 2. Demonstration 3 preserves the 8 on the rightward ray and continues beyond it.
Sources fill their rows and columns in their own colours, with overlaps coloured 2. Demonstration 1 overwrites the 8 in the 4 source's row with 4 while retaining the 8 outside all rays.
Demonstration 2 fills the 4 column with 4 and the shared column of two 1 sources with 2 except at the sources. Demonstration 3 similarly makes 2 below the aligned 4 and 3.
Demonstration 1 fills the rows and columns of 2 and 4, marking their intersections 6. Demonstration 3 preserves both 8 obstacles while rays continue beyond them.
Demonstration 1 fills the lone 3 source's row with 3, while the row containing two 4 sources becomes 2 except at the sources. Demonstration 3 shows the same overlap rule for two 1 sources.
Demonstration 1 colours the shared row of 3 and 1 with 6 except at sources. Its lone lower 1 paints both ways past an 8, preserving the 8 and filling the remaining row with 1.
